The right choice depends on your circumstances, growth plans, and appetite for administration — it's worth getting advice before you register anything.

Considerations when starting a business.summary: The practical groundwork worth doing before you start trading — from structure and funding to registrations and record-keeping.
body: Beyond the idea itself, starting a business well means settling a handful of practical questions early: what legal structure to trade under, how you'll fund the first months before revenue arrives, what registrations and licences you need, and what records you're required to keep from day one.

Getting these right from the outset avoids expensive corrections later — restructuring after the fact, or reconstructing a year of missing bookkeeping, both cost far more than doing it properly at the start. We work with new business owners through exactly this groundwork before they take their first order.

Could I really make a go of it?.summary: An honest look at what it takes to know whether a business idea is genuinely viable before you commit to it.
body: Enthusiasm for an idea is not the same as evidence it will work. A realistic assessment means testing your assumptions about demand, pricing, and costs against actual numbers — not just against your own confidence — and being honest about what you don't yet know.

It also means being clear-eyed about what running a business actually demands: cash flow through the quiet periods, the skills you'll need beyond your core expertise, and how much risk you can genuinely absorb. We help prospective business owners pressure-test their numbers before they hand in their notice, not after.

Credit control.summary: How to get paid on time and manage the risk of customers who don't pay, which is often what actually sinks a growing business.
body: More businesses run into trouble from slow-paying customers than from lack of demand — profitable on paper, but short of cash because invoices sit unpaid. Good credit control means setting clear payment terms upfront, checking a new customer's creditworthiness before extending credit, and following up on overdue invoices promptly and consistently rather than hoping they'll settle themselves.

It also means knowing when to say no — walking away from an order rather than taking on a customer who is unlikely to pay. We help clients put a credit control process in place that protects cash flow without damaging customer relationships.

Insuring your business.summary: The types of business insurance worth considering, and why the right cover depends heavily on what your business actually does.
body: The insurance a business needs varies enormously by what it does and who it deals with — public liability, professional indemnity, employers' liability, and cover for premises, stock, or key individuals all address different risks. Some are a legal requirement the moment you employ anyone; others are simply prudent given what you'd lose without them.

Under-insuring to save on premiums is a common false economy, but so is paying for cover you don't need. We can point clients toward the right conversations with a broker once we understand the shape of the business and where its real exposure sits.

Raising finance.summary: The main routes available for funding a business, from your own resources through to external investors, and how to prepare for each.
body: Options range from self-funding and family loans, through bank finance and asset-based lending, to equity investment from angels or venture capital. Each comes with a different cost, a different level of control you give up, and a different set of expectations about the numbers you'll need to show.

Whichever route you're pursuing, lenders and investors will want credible financial projections and a clear story about how the money will be used and repaid or returned. We help clients build the financial case that supports the conversation, not just the pitch.

Sources of finance.summary: A look at where business funding actually comes from — bank lending, alternative finance, grants, and investment — and what suits different stages of growth.
body: Beyond a straightforward bank loan, businesses can draw on invoice finance, asset finance, alternative lenders, government-backed schemes, and grants aimed at specific sectors or activities, alongside equity investment for higher-growth ventures. The right source depends on what the money is for and how quickly you need it.

Matching the type of finance to the purpose matters: funding day-to-day working capital with long-term debt, or funding equipment with short-term borrowing, both create avoidable strain later. We help clients work out which combination of sources actually fits their situation.

VAT - a summary.summary: An overview of how VAT works, when a business needs to register, and the broad obligations that come with being VAT registered.
body: VAT is charged on most goods and services sold in the UK, collected by registered businesses on HMRC's behalf. Once a business's taxable turnover passes the registration threshold it must register, charge VAT on its sales, and can generally reclaim VAT it has paid on business purchases, accounting for the difference to HMRC.

Registration brings ongoing obligations — charging the right rate, keeping proper records, and filing returns on schedule — and there are several accounting schemes that can simplify this depending on the size and nature of the business. We help clients register at the right time and choose a scheme that fits how they actually operate.

VAT - annual accounting scheme.summary: How the annual accounting scheme lets eligible businesses file one VAT return a year instead of quarterly, smoothing cash flow through instalments.
body: Rather than filing four VAT returns a year, businesses on this scheme submit one annual return and make regular advance payments toward their VAT bill throughout the year, based on an estimate. This reduces the administrative burden of quarterly filing and can make cash flow more predictable.

It suits businesses with stable, predictable turnover who'd rather budget for VAT in regular instalments than face a single larger reconciliation each quarter. It's not right for every business, particularly those expecting to reclaim more VAT than they charge — we help clients weigh that up before opting in.

VAT - bad debt relief.summary: How a VAT-registered business can reclaim the VAT already paid over to HMRC on invoices that a customer never actually pays.
body: When a business has accounted for VAT on a sale but the customer subsequently fails to pay, bad debt relief allows the VAT already handed over to HMRC on that invoice to be reclaimed, provided certain conditions and time limits are met.

Getting this right means keeping clear records of the original sale, the VAT accounted for, and the steps taken to recover the debt before writing it off. We help clients identify when relief is available and make sure it's claimed correctly rather than left on the table.

VAT - cash accounting.summary: How the cash accounting scheme lets eligible businesses account for VAT when payment is actually received or made, rather than on invoice dates.
body: Under standard VAT accounting, VAT is due based on invoice dates regardless of when payment is actually received. The cash accounting scheme instead lets eligible businesses account for VAT when money actually changes hands — which can meaningfully help cash flow, particularly where customers are slow to pay.

It also has a natural advantage if a customer never pays at all, since VAT was never due on that sale in the first place, avoiding the separate bad debt relief process. We help clients assess whether this scheme suits their payment patterns better than standard accounting.

VAT - flat rate scheme.summary: How the flat rate scheme simplifies VAT for smaller businesses by applying a single fixed percentage to turnover instead of tracking VAT on every purchase.
body: Rather than reclaiming VAT on individual purchases, businesses on the flat rate scheme apply a fixed percentage — set according to their trade sector — to their VAT-inclusive turnover and pay that over to HMRC. This significantly reduces the record-keeping burden of standard VAT accounting.

Whether it actually saves money depends on the sector rate and how much VAT-bearing expenditure the business has, so it doesn't suit everyone equally. We help clients run the comparison against standard accounting before deciding whether to join.

VAT - Making Tax Digital.summary: What Making Tax Digital for VAT requires — digital record-keeping and return filing through compatible software rather than manual submission.
body: Making Tax Digital requires VAT-registered businesses to keep their VAT records digitally and submit returns to HMRC through compatible software, rather than typing figures directly into HMRC's portal. The aim is fewer manual transcription errors and a more accurate, real-time link between a business's records and HMRC's systems.

In practice this means using accounting software, or bridging software linked to a spreadsheet, that connects directly to HMRC. We help clients get the right setup in place and keep their digital records compliant, so filing is routine rather than a quarterly scramble.

VAT - seven key points for the smaller b.summary: The practical VAT basics smaller businesses most often get caught out by, from registration timing to record-keeping and scheme choice.
body: Smaller businesses tend to trip up on the same handful of VAT points: registering too late (or too early), charging the wrong rate on certain goods or services, not keeping VAT invoices properly, and missing the right accounting scheme for how they actually trade. Each is straightforward to avoid once you know to look for it.

Getting comfortable with VAT early — registration, invoicing, record-keeping, filing deadlines, and scheme choice — saves far more time than sorting out mistakes retrospectively. We talk new and growing businesses through exactly these points so VAT becomes routine rather than a source of surprises.
